newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban withstand assault to hold key Afghan pass.
newsitem.headline: Taleban withstand assault to hold key Afghan pass.

text.p: Taleban troops held on to a strategic pass north of Kabul on Sunday despite an assault by ousted Afghan government forces using rockets, artillery and warplanes to try to dislodge them.
Fighting died down in the afternoon but intermittent shells and rockets continued to kick up the dust on the De Sabz pass, about 30 km (20 miles) north of the Afghan capital.

"We captured the high points which were planned," Abdullah, spokesman for ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, told reporters in the town of Jabal Os-Siraj, 90 km (60 miles) north of Kabul. "But the whole pass has not been secured," he said.
Abdullah said anti-Taleban forces suffered six wounded during the assault.
Earlier in the day, General Abdul Rauf Begi commanded the attack from a mud-walled compound in Tutakhon, back from the De Sabz pass.

"You can see for yourself, there's a war on," snapped the general, waving away reporters as he directed fire using a walkie-talkie and glanced at a Russian map of the area splayed out in front of him on the mud wall of a turret.
Shells and rockets exploded on the barren mountainside every minute early on Sunday, flashing orange and sending up plumes of thick, yellow dust.
A uniformed orderly stood by the general with a tray of cool green grapes, oblivious to the low thump of outgoing artillery.
The general wore an olive green kepi, the trademark of a commander belonging to forces of the northern Uzbek leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Masood's former government forces have allied with Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli faction in a bid to drive the radical Islamic Taleban militia out of Kabul. The Taleban captured the city one month ago on Sunday, giving it control of over two-thirds of the country.
Masood's commanders at the front said warplanes belonging to Dostum flew two sorties over Taleban positions early on Sunday and confirmed they had also bombed Kabul airport.
Abdullah said he had no details of Dostum warplanes hitting residential areas in Kabul. "According to our information, the target was only the airport (in Kabul)."
The assault was the anti-Taleban alliance's second try in less than a week at forcing the Taleban off the pass.
Their forces are ranged out on highly exposed ground below the De Sabz pass, where their armour and men stand out against the desert sand and pale green camelthorn.
"We are exposed, it is a problem," said an alliance source in Tutakhon.
A jeep with a multi-barrelled rocket launcher mounted on the back sped past in a whirl of dust towards the frontline, the chequered headcloths of the fighters flapping violently in the wind.
There was sporadic return fire from Taleban troops while Taleban jetfighters occasionally bombed from the air.
A representative with the aid organisation Medicins Sans Frontieres in Jabal Os-Siraj said five people were lightly wounded when a Taleban jet bombed the town on Sunday morning.
